Chapter 12
Quality Notification
The goal of problem notification should be to form a business workflow
across several specialist departments. The main task of the notification
system is to handle external and internal complaints in connection with
suppliers and customers, as well as trace problems in the production
processes.
The communication of quality-related complaints is one of the touchstones of every
company’s customer-supplier relationship, whether it’s internal or external. Compa-
nies examining the overall business context of complaints discover how a complaints
process requires the involvement of multiple areas: materials management (MM), pro-
duction planning (PP), SAP S/4HANA Sales, and, of course, QM. This results primarily in
the need for a smooth notification processing workflow supported by suitable tools,
such as automated notification systems.
In this chapter, we’ll provide a comprehensive example that’s based on logistic core pro-
cesses, and the same principles can be put to use without great difficulty in all commer-
cial implementation areas, whether they are trade, production, or service areas. This
example will highlight the business needs and technical requirements of quality notifi-
cations. We’ll first provide an overview of how quality notification works within a work-
flow in general and set up our example, then discuss how the different SAP S/4HANA
areas use quality notification, and finally delve into the different tools you can use for
specific tasks. Although this chapter will show a customer complaint that triggers qual-
ity notification creation, companies can also leverage quality notifications for attending
to nonconformance or initiating corrective and preventive actions, which is also dis-
cussed in this chapter.
12.1 Workflow
In general, several areas and employees of the company are involved in processing a
complaint. In the case of a customer complaint, the process moves from a company’s
external starting point through the processing by the addressee and returns to the
external starting point. This requires communication and coordination of all stake-
holders involved in handling complaints.

12 Quality Notification
524
At the outset, a complaint is assigned a number to ensure its clear identification and
tracking, supplemented with a reference object, such as the customer order, the cus-
tomer number, or the delivery number, and additional reference data. Ideally, the orga-
nizational responsibilities for further compliant processing are already in place, one
person is made the person in charge, and the others involved are assigned with clearly
defined tasks within a case of complaint. Basically, complaints processing is similar to
a small project with a defined starting point and a successful end.
The internal process requires fast and effective information distribution and an imme-
diate execution of corrective actions. The basis for correct decisions comes from both
experience and access to the knowledge acquired from complaint cases that were pre-
viously processed. The measures taken and the time necessary for performing these
actions is information that needs to be transferred rapidly and, most importantly, in
the correct form to the person who registered the complaint. Subsequently, the evalu-
ation of a complaint that has emerged provides important information on the weak-
nesses of the affected product and the performance of the company. The requirement
to fulfill all the detailed conditions gives you an idea of the complexity of the task.
As the use of quality notifications is generally seen in the context of poor quality or
nonquality, a few more aspects of active quality control with the SAP notification sys-
tem are as follows:
 Organization of the company notification system
 Coordination with the customers in terms of the QS 9000 requirements
 Support of processes that were initialized by the failure mode and effects analysis
(FMEA) team (see Chapter 16)
For the aforementioned areas, you can configure your own notification types from
those that are available in the standard SAP S/4HANA system to enable an effective
notification structure. There are many ways of tailoring each notification type so that
it meets the requirements of the business users. Table 12.1 provides quality notifica-
tions that are specific to QM and covers customer, in-house, and supplier complaint
types. The advantage of an integrated application is particularly strong with regard to
quality notifications because you can refer to all the logistics data that you’ll need to
effectively and efficiently process a customer’s complaint going through different
phases of corrective and rectification actions.

The example in this chapter stipulates that you’ve already processed and delivered a

demanding an immediate replacement delivery. You use a standard SAP notification
system to trace the case and perform a complete documentation and defects analysis.

The objective is to attend to the customer’s complaint as quickly as possible and avoid
a recurrence of the defect via proactive quality assurance. The processing flow we use
dictates that an incoming customer complaint is with reference to a sales document.
Because complaints usually arrive at customer services, the notification header and the
subject of the complaint may be filled out by the company’s customer services depart-
ment.
In the processing flow of this example, the quality department is responsible for all
subsequent data inputs and the completion of the notification. In this case, the respon-
sibility for tracing tasks in the area of QM also lies within the quality department. In
your company, you can organize the processing of complaints in a completely differ-
ent way. Therefore, we highly recommend that you thoroughly model the business
processes with all parties involved to ensure efficient and effective notification han-
dling.
12.2 Quality Notification in SAP S/4HANA Sales
This section covers the quality notification in SAP S/4HANA Sales and, more specifi-
cally, notification type Q1 (customer complaint). The functionalities and operations of
the different quality notifications are basically identical. The major differences can be
found in the reference objects of the header data and in the individual processing pro-
files. The partner schema contains separate partner roles for each notification type. We
recommend that you keep the mandatory partners as provided in the standard ver-
sion, as well as the customers (known as business partners in SAP S/4HANA) and the
responsible processors.
The following are the reference objects of the customer complaint notification type:

When you select specific reference objects through the initially displayed screen, the
system transfers additional data from a document (sales order, delivery) to the notifi-

The most important step in implementing this notification type is a straightforward
design of the business process. In most cases, the business user creates this notification
type after a telephone complaint or written complaint by the customer.
12.2.1 Creating a Quality Notification: Customer Complaint
To create a quality notification for a customer complaint, use Transaction QM01 or fol-
low menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Notification  Create. Then, for
Notification Type, choose Q1. A dialog box opens (see Figure 12.2) in which you can enter
the requested document numbers from the customer order or delivery.
Figure 12.2 Initial Screen of Quality Notification: Customer Complaint
You must also enter the item number here, or the system won’t be able to find the con-
tents of the document (e.g., the material ordered) and can’t transfer this data into the
notification.
When you press (Enter), the system transfers the most important document data for
the quality notification into the notification header (see Figure 12.3). The system
assigns the notification number in accordance with the settings of the number range
interval internally. By entering the related customer sales order, you obtain relevant

data such as purchase order number, material number, production date, delivery quan-
tity, and delivery date, depending on your system setting. If notifications already exist
for a customer or material, the system displays a message informing you of their exis-
tence and provides you with an overview of similar complaints with the same refer-
ence.
Figure 12.3 Quality Notification: Customer Complaint
All that’s required as the mandatory partner of the customer complaint is the name
of the customer who already has a master data record in the SAP S/4HANA system.
Depending on the configuration settings, it’s also possible to set other partners of the
notification as mandatory or optional.
The data that you see in the Reference Objects tab in Figure 12.3 relates to details of the
customer, supplier, or in-house information. For example, for a customer complaint,
there is a provision to enter all SAP S/4HANA Sales-related information about the cus-
tomer. This then acts as a cross-reference when you want to see the information in
reports and the information system. If you enter a material and its batch number, then
when you run notification or analysis reports, the system can come up with more pre-
cise and relevant information. Similarly, entering the sales order or its delivery infor-
mation (though it’s not mandatory) will eventually help you track the problem and its
associated notifications more precisely and accurately.

tify the error or defect, then you can enter the relevant details in the Costs and Account

12.2.2 Correction Tasks
You now deal with a targeted correction task for the notification item. Unlike the
immediate task, which we’ll describe later, this targeted correction task isn’t assigned

planned start and finish of each task and can therefore trace the current processing sta-
tus throughout the process (see Figure 12.8). You can also set the status of each notifica-
tion item of the task, such as Release, In-Process, or Complete, via the menu bar located
at the bottom of the screen.

12.2.3 Changing the Activities Status and Completing the Notification
After successfully performing tasks of items (activities), you process the status of
immediate and item tasks in the notification. Double-click a task in the tasks overview,
and you’ll see the detail view, where you can change the status of an item’s task
(Released, Completed, or Successful). First choose Completed; directly after that,
choose Successful. In Figure 12.14, at the bottom-right side of the screen (not shown),
you can maintain various statuses of a quality notification.
After performing all immediate tasks, you can select additional notification items and
the related tasks—for example, correction tasks—from the list and mark them as com-
pleted in the detail screen. A notification completion is possible only with completed
tasks. For this reason, you choose Notification  Functions  Complete  External Origin
(see Figure 12.15).
With this function, the notification receives the system statuses NOCO (notification

appears in gray and doesn’t allow any additional processing. However, in the same
menu path, you can reset the status of the notification to Put in Process, an option lim-

12.2.4 System Status and User Status
You can use two status forms for quality notification: the system status, with its stan-
dard profile already defined, and the user status, which can also be set. You can config-
ure the user status so that you can use it to override the system status manually. In

configuration, you create and assign the status profile and set up the structure of the
quality notifications.
12.2.5 Follow-On Action
With the follow-on action, you can automatically trigger system functions such as
extended quality inspections, changes to the supplier relationship, creating an addi-
tional notification, and other logistics processes. The function is selected in the task
detail from a catalog and is activated when you save the task. Basically, the follow-on
action is the start of a function module.
12.2.6 Action Log
The action log provides a detailed overview of all users’ actions for a quality notifica-
tion and is accessible via Extras  Notification Documents  Action Log (see Figure 12.16).

cess and the last notifications. Because the sales summary is an interactive report, you

12.2.7 Partner Data of the Notification
Partners are companies or individual persons who are involved in the context of the
notification. For example, suppliers and responsible processors are the mandatory
partners set for notification type Q2 (complaint against supplier), without which you
can’t save a notification. In the case of customer complaints, the customer and the
responsible employee are the mandatory partners. The mandatory partners of the
notification are entered on the Contact Person Address tab. Alternatively, you can enter
the partners in a selection list in the quality notification menu bar via Goto  Partner.
12.2.8 The 8D Report
The 8D problem solution methodology (also referred to as the eight-step plan) is a series
of eight steps (disciplines) that should be run through as soon as a problem emerges. If
handled correctly, this method helps in finding a timely and complete solution to the
problem in question. This method’s fact-oriented approach makes certain that solu-
tions, decisions, and planning are based on actual and reliable data, solving the core
problem instead of merely addressing the symptoms. Furthermore, the 8D report that
should accompany the process serves as a progress control and catalyst, which ensures
that all stakeholders involved in all steps and processes of the 8D process adhere to and
implement them. In other words, the 8D process is a problem management tool sup-
ported by a specific report form, thus specifying and ensuring a uniform standard for
companies and suppliers.
The 8D process was developed to increase the efficiency of problem-solving in the areas
of production and development. Ineffective problem-solving is generally caused by
some of the following factors:
 A clear description and focused definition isn’t already in place before a team can
effectively process a problem.
 In the problem-solving process, there is a general tendency to skip necessary steps in
an attempt to quickly find a solution.
 Not all members of the team may be actively cooperating or participating, which
means that the team may not be able to record all causes of the problem.
 There may not be a systematic approach for setting priorities, performing analyses,
and investigating the problem.
 The persons involved lack the technical skills and know-how required to use the
tools and implement the working techniques that support the problem solution
process.

538
 Due to a lack of technical or functional knowledge of the problem and solution pro-
cess, as well as an underestimation of the required work, management sets unrealis-
tic deadlines. This forces the teams to lean toward insufficient analyses.
 Sometimes, a possible cause of the problem is accepted too readily as the basic
cause, and the investigation of the problem ends. However, later the problem comes
up again because the actual cause wasn’t properly clarified.
 Although the basic cause of the problem may have been identified, insufficient or
even temporary improvement tasks were initiated. For permanent improvement
tasks to be effective, support on the part of management for approving costs and
implementing tasks is required but wasn’t granted or approved.
 There isn’t enough information available on the same problem or on similar prob-
lems that might have previously occurred.
The eight steps (8D) to resolve the problem are as follows:
1. Define the problem of the internal or external customer as precisely as possible.
2. Work out the root cause of the problem and quantify it. Collect and analyze statisti-
cal data.
3. Initiate tasks that, where possible, keep the effects of problems of internal or exter-
nal customers on hold until a permanent solution is found. Constantly check the
effectiveness of these temporary tasks, and, if necessary, implement additional
tasks.
4. Determine whether the problem can be solved. Search for all possible root causes
that could explain the occurrence of the problem. Determine the possible cause(s),
and check via comparisons with the problem description and existing data whether
a likely cause is a basic cause. Validate and confirm your assumptions with tests and
experiments.
5. Search for all possible tasks that could eliminate the cause(s) and solve the problem.
Choose the optimal permanent improvement task(s) and prove by means of appro-
priate tests that the selected permanent improvement tasks really solve the prob-
lem and don’t have any undesirable side effects.
6. Create an action plan to implement the selected improvement task(s), and deter-
mine which controls will ensure that the cause of the problem is completely elimi-
nated. Implement the action plan, observe the effects, and, if necessary, execute the
tasks provided for possible scenarios.
7. Change the management and control systems, instructions, and usual processes to
avoid a recurrence of the same or similar problems. Identify improvement possibil-
ities and initiate process improvement tasks.
8. The quality department head acknowledges the completion of the 8D report by sign-
ing and dating the notification completion.

12.3 Quality Notification in Production
This section covers quality notifications in production and, more specifically, notifica-
tion type Q3 (internal problem notification). An internal problem notification refers to
problems that emerge within your company’s production processes (e.g., defects in a
material or an operation during the production process). Additional areas of use are
events that take place in the company and that are to be traced immediately, for which
actions need to be taken. The internal notification for a production order can directly
trigger a supplier fault list and change the quality score of the supplier.

The following are the reference objects of the internal problem notification type:
 Internal partner
 Material, batch
 Production order (or process order)
or run schedule header
 Work center
 Inspection lot
 Author (mandatory partner)
You can create notifications for production through manual and automatic functions
and through initialization from other QM components—for example, through the
usage decision or the inspection lot in the event of a defect. The internal problem noti-
fication (see Figure 12.18 and Figure 12.19) refers to occurrences of nonconformity in the
company. The two most important reference objects are the production (or process)
order and the inspection order. The processing logic is the same here as with the other
notification types in QM.
Figure 12.18 Notification: Internal Problem (Production)
During the inspection, the line supervisor classifies the defect on its discovery. You can
perform this classification by having the inspection task prompt you to enter a pre-
defined defect code, if the evaluation result includes a defect. Then, the quality inspec-
tor simply selects an applicable defect code and completes the inspection step. This

12.4 Quality Notification in Procurement
Let’s look at the quality notification in procurement. The relevant notification type is
Q2, which denotes the complaint against the supplier and the supplier fault list, respec-
tively. The buyer’s negotiation sheet enables the company to evaluate a supplier’s or
supplier’s price, quality, and delivery performance and assess other key performance
indicators to decide how best to move forward with the business relationship. The doc-
ument flow maintains an end-to-end link of the quality notification and its associated
objects in a graphical form.
12.4.1 Create a Quality Notification
Notification type Q2 processes and manages complaints against suppliers or other
external partners. With the supplier fault list, QM provides a comprehensive tool for
quality control in MM. In addition to the standard functions, the created notifications
can also influence the supplier evaluation and record cost analyses for expenses
related to the supplier fault lists. (You can find more information about supplier evalu-
ations in Chapter 19, Section 19.1.)

12.6 Corrective and Preventive Action
A formal and an organized correction process can help a company better manage
defect reporting and improve related workflows. The key elements of an integrated cor-
rective and preventive action system include continuous monitoring based on docu-
mented procedures, prioritization and risk management, verification and validation,
and well-defined procedures. The define, measure, analyze, improve, and control
(DMAIC) framework is a business methodology that helps track down and mitigate the
root causes of defects. Using DMAIC, a problem is defined, performance of an area or
process is measured, analysis of the process is undertaken, improvements are made
based on the analysis, and finally controls are put in place for the amended processes.
In an ever-competitive environment, a majority of industries are facing increasing
pressure from regulatory bodies, the latest customer mandates, and internal quality
initiatives to engage a proactive and automated approach for managing nonconfor-
mity, process deviations, and critical observations in relation to the defined quality
procedures across their supply chains.
Corrective and preventive action is one such process that has become a formal require-
ment by regulatory authorities for categorizing the various types of issues a company
may encounter. The corrective and preventive action process described in this section
is based on the DMAIC framework, which can significantly improve supply chain per-
formance by addressing critical-to-quality problems, including the following:
 Nonconformity incidents, which are deviations from processes and procedures that
are detected during audits (audits can be conducted internally or by external regula-
tory bodies)
 Process-related incidents resulting from an internal or external audit at a supplier
premise
 Complaints from customers
Corrective and preventive action can help organizations identify, record, investigate,
and resolve nonconformity issues across the supply chain. Apart from resolving inci-
dents within the organization with regard to process inconsistencies reported by cus-
tomers or any other internal process issue, the corrective and preventive action process

based on the DMAIC framework can also help assess supplier process compliance during
delivery of goods and services.
The corrective and preventive action process requires companies to document the
issues, monitor the progress and impact of the actions taken, and implement the find-
ings to prevent reoccurrence of the major cause of the complaint and to improve pro-
cess quality. Companies can then use these findings to conduct largely error-free
operations and to make informed decisions that result in higher quality and more reli-
able supply chain operations. Corrective and preventive action can be implemented in
any industry.
For instance, companies can initiate corrective and preventive action with an investiga-
tion to identify the root cause of the nonconformance. Root-cause analysis centers on
ascertaining the source of a problem, defect, or nonconformity by identifying the rea-
sons for a product failure or inconsistency in process operations. From there, corrective
or preventive action to address the issue can be implemented. Corrective and preven-

12.8.7 Defects Recording
For different notification types, you can set up recording of different defects using con-
firmation profiles. Confirmation profiles define the contents of the defect records. For
each inspection type, you must assign appropriate notification types to properly
record the defects. You can assign defects at the inspection lot level, the operation level,
or the master inspection characteristic level.
The system can also trigger automatic defect recording if the appropriate control indi-
cator is set and the defect code is entered from catalog 9 in the catalog data. The busi-
ness users set the characteristic as rejected if the results of the quality inspection reveal
that tolerance levels are exceeded. Such recorded defects can generate appropriate
quality notifications. You can also manually record defects at any time.
To set the necessary configuration settings for defects recording and associated notifi-
cation types, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications 
Defects Recording  Define Notification Types.
Choose the appropriate inspection type, such as inspection type 04. Here, you can
assign notification type F3, and the system manually or automatically creates notifica-
tions (depending on the other settings) whenever the business user records defects for
inspection type 04. Inspection type 04 is relevant for goods receipt against production
or process orders.
